Read About Zanzibar

An island that traded on the monsoon winds for a thousand years, and still carries every culture that trade ever brought ashore.

A city built by the wind

Stone Town exists because of the monsoon. For half the year the kaskazi wind blows from the northeast, carrying dhows down from Arabia, Persia and India; for the other half the kusi blows from the southeast, carrying them home again. Sailors who timed the crossing right could sail to Zanzibar on one wind and leave on the other, and for over a thousand years that single fact of geography turned a modest coral island off the coast of East Africa into one of the busiest trading ports on the Indian Ocean. Everyone who came on those winds left something behind — language, food, architecture, religion — and Stone Town is what a millennium of that leaves standing.

The result is not a African city with foreign influences bolted on, nor an Arab city that happens to sit in Africa. It is genuinely both at once, fused closely enough that Swahili culture itself — the language, the coastal civilization that stretches from Somalia to Mozambique — took its name from the Arabic word for "coast," sawahil, and its grammar from Bantu Africa. Zanzibar was never a colony grafted onto a native population in the way that word usually implies. It was the place where those populations had already been mixing for a thousand years before any European ship arrived.

Sultans, cloves, and an empire that moved

In 1832, Sultan Said bin Sultan of Oman did something almost no ruler in history has done voluntarily: he moved his entire capital. Zanzibar was more valuable to him than Muscat, so he relocated the seat of the Omani Empire to Stone Town and never looked back. Under his rule the island became the world's leading producer of cloves, planted on plantations like the one at Kizimbani that still operates today, and Stone Town's harbor became the central exchange point for ivory, slaves and spices moving between the African interior and the markets of Asia and Europe.

The wealth built the city that survives now — the House of Wonders with its cast-iron columns imported from Glasgow and its status as the first building in East Africa with electricity, the Old Fort built by Omani forces after they expelled the Portuguese in 1699, the merchant houses along the harborfront with their carved teak doors, each door pattern signaling the owner's origin and status to anyone who could read the carving. Brass studs on a door meant an Indian merchant family, expecting to deter war elephants back in Gujarat — an ornamental habit imported wholesale to an island that had never seen an elephant near its coast.

The wealth that built Stone Town's most beautiful buildings was extracted from the worst thing that happened on this island.

The trade the city cannot forget

Stone Town's prosperity had a source that the city does not hide from. Under Omani rule Zanzibar became the largest slave-trading port on the eastern coast of Africa, the terminus for caravan routes that reached as far inland as the Congo. An estimated 600,000 to 900,000 people passed through Zanzibar's slave market over the course of the nineteenth century before Britain forced its closure in 1873, using its naval dominance of the Indian Ocean as leverage against a sultanate that depended on British protection.

The market itself stood on the site now occupied by Christ Church Cathedral, consecrated in 1879 on the exact ground where captives had been sold, its altar deliberately placed over the location of the old whipping post. The underground holding chambers survive beneath the cathedral, low-ceilinged rooms where people were held before sale, and they are kept open specifically so the history stays visible rather than buried under a more comfortable story. It is not the only slave-trading port in history to build a monument on its own site of atrocity, but the directness of the placement — worship literally standing on top of the wound — is unusual, and it is the reason the cathedral draws visitors who come for history rather than religion.

A revolution that ended an era in a single week

Zanzibar's sultanate outlasted the slave trade by nearly a century, surviving as a British protectorate until it gained independence in December 1963. The independent sultanate lasted barely a month longer. In January 1964, a Ugandan-born self-proclaimed field marshal named John Okello led an uprising that overthrew the Arab-dominated government in a matter of days, ending centuries of Omani rule and killing thousands in the process — the exact death toll is still disputed, with estimates ranging from the low thousands to over ten thousand. A few months later Zanzibar merged with mainland Tanganyika to form Tanzania, a union that Zanzibar retains its own president, parliament and semi-autonomous status within to this day.

The revolution emptied much of Stone Town's Arab and Indian merchant class within a generation, and the grand houses they left behind fell into disrepair for decades before restoration efforts — driven substantially by UNESCO World Heritage status, granted in 2000 — began bringing them back. Walk through Stone Town today and the layering is visible in the buildings themselves: original 19th-century Omani stonework, mid-20th-century neglect, and 21st-century restoration, sometimes all three in the same façade.

The rock star nobody in Stone Town claimed for decades

Farrokh Bulsara was born in Stone Town in 1946 to Parsi parents from India, in a house on Kenyatta Road that the family left for good after the 1964 revolution, when the new government's targeting of the island's Indian and Arab minorities made staying untenable. The family relocated to England, where Farrokh became Freddie Mercury and eventually the frontman of Queen — a fact Zanzibar itself was slow to embrace. For years the island's tourism industry was cautious about celebrating a gay, Parsi, non-Muslim icon on a 95%-Muslim island, and it was really international fan pilgrimage, more than local initiative, that turned the Kenyatta Road house into the small museum it is today. The bar named for him on the seafront came later still. It is now one of the most photographed addresses in Stone Town, a small, slightly incongruous footnote to a much older story about who has passed through this island and what they left.

Beyond the old town

Stone Town is Zanzibar's history, but it is not the whole island. North of the city the interior opens into the plantations that gave Zanzibar its old nickname, "Spice Island" — clove, nutmeg, cardamom and vanilla still grown on working farms like Kizimbani, walked with guides who crack open pods and bark to demonstrate what each spice smells like raw. East and south of Stone Town, Jozani-Chwaka Bay is the island's only national park and the last significant habitat of the Zanzibar red colobus monkey, a subspecies found nowhere else on earth, alongside a mangrove boardwalk through the tidal creek that separates the forest from the bay.

The north coast at Nungwi and the beaches at Kendwa are a different Zanzibar again — the one built for the tide rather than the trade wind, since Kendwa's deep-water beach stays swimmable at any point in the tidal cycle while Nungwi's reef-fringed shoreline strands swimmers at low tide. Offshore, Mnemba Atoll's protected reef is generally reckoned the best snorkeling and diving in the archipelago, close enough to shore for a half-day trip and clear enough that the coral is visible from the boat before anyone gets in the water.

None of it explains Zanzibar on its own. The island only makes sense as the sum of the parts: a trading post that became a sultanate's capital, a capital built on a trade the world eventually judged unforgivable, a revolution that ended it all in a week, and an afterlife spent restoring what survived. Stone Town's carved doors, its cathedral over the slave market, its cast-iron colonial ironwork, its call to prayer echoing off Omani stonework — none of it is decoration. It's what a thousand years of monsoon trade actually looks like, still standing.
